'''John William Scott''' "'''Ian'''" '''Cassels''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name="Fellow Royal Society">{{Cite journal |last1=Dietmann |first1=Rainer |last2=Fisher |first2=Tom |last3=Smyth |first3=Chris |last4=Velani |first4=Sanju |date=2023 |title=John William Scott ('Ian') Cassels. 11 July 1922 — 27 July 2015 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=74|pages=87–108 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2022.0035 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (11 July 1922 &ndash; 27 July 2015<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://listserv.nodak.edu/cgi-bin/wa.exe?A2=NMBRTHRY;b55dbdac.1508|title = LISTSERV - NMBRTHRY Archives - LISTSERV.NODAK.EDU}}</ref>) was a British mathematician.

==Biography==
Cassels was educated at Neville's Cross Council School in [[Durham, England|Durham]] and [[George Heriot's School]] in Edinburgh. He went on to study at the [[University of Edinburgh]] and graduated with an undergraduate [[Master of Arts (Scotland)|Master of Arts]] (MA) degree in 1943.

His academic career was interrupted in [[World War II]] when he was involved in [[cryptography]] at [[Bletchley Park]]. After the war he became a research student of [[Louis Mordell]] at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]]; he received his PhD in 1949 and was elected a [[Fellow#Oxford, Cambridge and Dublin|fellow]] of Trinity in the same year.

Cassels then spent a year lecturing in mathematics at the [[University of Manchester]] before returning to Cambridge as a lecturer in 1950. He was appointed [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] in Arithmetic in 1963, the same year he was elected as a fellow of the [[Royal Society of London]]. In 1967 he was appointed as [[Sadleirian Professor of Pure Mathematics]] at Cambridge. In 1969 he became Head of the [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge|Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics]]. He retired in 1984.

==Mathematical work==
He initially worked on [[elliptic curve]]s. After a period when he worked on [[geometry of numbers]] and [[diophantine approximation]], he returned in the later 1950s to the arithmetic of elliptic curves, writing a series of papers connecting the [[Selmer group]] with [[Galois cohomology]] and laying some of the foundations of the modern theory of [[infinite descent]].<ref name="Fellow Royal Society"/> His best-known single result may be the proof that the [[Tate-Shafarevich group]] of an elliptic curve, if it is finite, must have order that is a square; the proof being by construction of an [[alternating form]].

Cassels often studied individual [[Diophantine equation]]s by [[algebraic number theory]] and [[p-adic methods]].

His publications include 200 papers. His advanced textbooks have influenced generations of mathematicians; some of Cassels's books have remained in print for decades.
